Ark of the Covenant
ARK of the KUV-uh-nunt
n. phrase
Ark from Latin arca (a chest); covenant from Latin convenire (to come together). Hebrew ’arōn ha-b’rīth, “chest of the covenant”; the gold-overlaid acacia-wood chest that held the tablets of the covenant in the most holy place.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Ark of the Covenant was the most sacred object of Old Testament Israel—a gold-overlaid acacia-wood chest, approximately 3.75 feet long by 2.25 feet wide by 2.25 feet high (2.5 x 1.5 x 1.5 cubits), placed in the most holy place of the tabernacle (and subsequently the temple) as the throne of God’s manifest presence among His people. Exodus 25:10-22 prescribes its construction. The chest contained three items: the two stone tablets of the covenant on which God wrote the Ten Commandments with His own finger (Ex 25:16; Deut 10:5); a golden pot of manna (Heb 9:4); and Aaron’s rod that budded (Heb 9:4). The lid was the mercy seat (kapporeth, propitiatory), with two cherubim of beaten gold rising from the ends of the mercy seat with their wings stretching upward and their faces toward each other and toward the mercy seat. The LORD’s presence was manifested above the mercy seat between the cherubim: and there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim which are upon the ark of the testimony, of all things which I will give thee in commandment unto the children of Israel (Ex 25:22). The Ark structures several biblical theological themes. It is the throne-symbol of God’s presence among His people; the place of meeting and revelation; the seat of atonement (where the high priest sprinkled the blood of atonement on the Day of Atonement); the deposit-place of the covenantal Law-tablets, manna, and budded rod (each carrying its own theological significance: Law as the standard, manna as the LORD’s provision in the wilderness, Aaron’s rod as the divine vindication of the priestly order); and the battle-emblem under which Israel went forth to victory in the conquest. Its history is dramatic. Captured by the Philistines after Eli’s sons disgraced themselves (1 Sam 4-6); recovered with judgments upon the Philistines and finally upon the men of Bethshemesh who looked into it; brought up to Jerusalem by David with great rejoicing (2 Sam 6; 1 Chr 13, 15); installed in Solomon’s temple in the most holy place (1 Kgs 8); lost to history at some point before the Babylonian captivity (its fate is uncertain). Hebrews 9 makes the typological argument explicit. The Ark and its contents are the patterns of things in the heavens; the true tabernacle is the heavenly one; Christ has entered, not into the earthly holy place made with hands, but into heaven itself, into the presence of God for us, with His own blood. The Ark of the Covenant is therefore one of the central typological emblems of the Old Testament, pointing to the presence of God Himself, mediated through Christ’s atoning blood, applied to the saints by the eternal Spirit.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ARK as a chest; in scripture, the sacred chest that held the tablets of the covenant, the pot of manna, and Aaron’s rod that budded; placed in the most holy place of the tabernacle and temple as the throne of God’s manifest presence among His people.

expand to see more

ARK, n. — 1. A small close vessel, chest or coffer. 2. Among the Jews, the sacred coffer or chest which contained the two tables of the testimony, sometimes called the ark of the covenant, ark of the testimony, ark of the LORD, ark of God. It was made of shittim wood, overlaid with gold, and stood in the most holy place of the tabernacle.

COVENANT, n. — In law, a mutual agreement; in theology, the various special arrangements by which God brings men into relation with Himself, of which the tablets in the ark were the foundational testimony.

📖 Key Scripture

Exodus 25:21-22 — "And thou shalt put the mercy seat above upon the ark; and in the ark thou shalt put the testimony that I shall give thee. And there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim..."

Hebrews 9:3-5 — "And after the second veil, the tabernacle which is called the Holiest of all; Which had the golden censer, and the ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold, wherein was the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron’s rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant; And over it the cherubims of glory shadowing the mercyseat..."

1 Samuel 4:21-22 — "And she named the child Ichabod, saying, The glory is departed from Israel: because the ark of God was taken... And she said, The glory is departed from Israel: for the ark of God is taken."

Hebrews 9:11-12 — "But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this building; Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Ark of the Covenant doctrine is corrupted by the speculative-quest pattern that has, especially in modern times, treated the Ark chiefly as a lost artifact to be located through archeology or apocalyptic speculation—and by the inverse loss of typological reading that has reduced the Ark to ancient cultic curiosity without tracing its Christological substance in Hebrews 9.

expand to see more

The speculative-quest pattern—Indiana Jones popular and the various modern claims to have located the Ark in Mount Sinai, in Ethiopia, in the Temple Mount—has captured the contemporary imagination of the Ark as a lost-artifact to be physically recovered. The biblical writers’ treatment is different. The Old Testament prophets (Jer 3:16, prophesying of a coming time when the Ark shall not come to mind: neither shall they remember it; neither shall they visit it; neither shall that be done any more) and the New Testament writers (especially Hebrews 9) treat the Ark’s physical history as having served its purpose, with its substantive realities now fulfilled in Christ. The Ark itself, whether lost or hidden or destroyed in the Babylonian destruction, is no longer the church’s focus; the Christ to whom the Ark pointed is. The recovery is the recovery of the typological reading, with the Ark’s historical fate as a secondary curiosity and its Christological substance as the primary theological lesson.

The opposite corruption is the general loss of typological reading that has reduced the Ark to ancient cultic curiosity without tracing its Christological substance in Hebrews 9. The Ark’s theological wealth—throne of God’s presence, seat of atonement, deposit of the Law-tablets, the manna, and Aaron’s rod, the place of meeting between God and His people—is rich with Christological substance the apostles drew out. Christ is the true mercy seat (Rom 3:25, the word hilastērion is the LXX word for mercy-seat); Christ has entered the true holy place (the heavenly, of which the earthly was a pattern); Christ has obtained eternal redemption by His own blood (as the Aaronic high priest entered the holy place once a year with the blood of bulls and goats). The recovery of the Ark-typology is the recovery of one of the deepest and most pastoral lines of NT theology: the presence of God among His people, mediated through Christ’s atoning blood, applied by the eternal Spirit—the substantive reality of which the Ark of the Covenant was the prophetic shadow.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ’arōn ha-b’rīth (chest of the covenant); the gold-overlaid acacia-wood chest in the most holy place of tabernacle and temple, containing the Law-tablets, the manna, and Aaron’s rod; throne of God’s manifest presence; typologically fulfilled in Christ who has entered the true heavenly holy place with His own blood (Heb 9).

expand to see more

Hebrew ’arōn (H727) — chest, ark.

Hebrew b’rīth (H1285) — covenant.

Greek kibōtos (G2787) — ark, chest (NT term; Heb 9:4; Rev 11:19).

Greek hilastērion (G2435) — propitiatory, mercy-seat (LXX of kapporeth; applied to Christ in Rom 3:25).
